input_contract.description: A single signed 32-bit integer x. The statement says the value may be negative or positive, and requires 0 to be returned when the REVERSED value leaves the signed 32-bit range - so the problem is overflow-sensitive on its output, not its input. Not a sequence, so duplicate and ordering categories do not apply.

mutants.description: reverses the magnitude correctly but never reapplies the sign, so every negative input returns a positive result
reverses and returns without any range check, ignoring the statement's third rule entirely
saturates at the 32-bit boundary instead of returning 0, the standard saturating-arithmetic reflex
range-checks x rather than the reversed value, so the guard can never fire on a valid input
digit-extraction loop conditioned on n > 0, so it never executes for a negative input and returns 0
mechanical: the overflow branch returns None instead of 0, which the harness renders as an empty line
mechanical: the sign ternary is inverted, negating every result
mechanical: the int() normalisation is dropped, so a trailing zero survives as a leading zero in the rendered output

t1-drops-the-sign.why_wrong: The statement's second worked example is exactly this case. Taking abs() to make the string reversal work and then forgetting to restore the sign is the single most common way this problem is got wrong, because the magnitude logic looks finished and tests on positive inputs all pass.

t1-no-overflow-guard.why_wrong: Implements the two obligations a reader notices - reverse the digits, keep the sign - and skips the third, which is stated in one short sentence at the end. In Python nothing forces the issue: integers do not overflow, so the omission is invisible until an input whose reversal exceeds the range.

t1-clamps-to-int-max.why_wrong: Reads 'overflows' and reaches for saturating arithmetic, which is what hardware and many libraries do. The statement instead specifies a sentinel: return 0. The author has noticed the rule and applied the wrong remedy, which is a more advanced mistake than missing it.

t1-guards-the-input-not-the-result.why_wrong: Places a correct-looking bounds check on the wrong value. x is a valid 32-bit integer by precondition, so this guard can never fire, and the code reads as though the rule is handled. Guarding the input rather than the output is a recognised defensive-programming reflex.

t1-loop-assumes-positive-input.why_wrong: The digit-extraction loop is the standard arithmetic solution, written with `while n > 0` because digits are naturally thought of as positive. It silently returns 0 for every negative input. The `!= 0` form a C or Java author would reach for instead does not terminate in Python, where -1 // 10 is -1 - which is why this variant, not that one, is the realistic Python misconception.

t2-returns-none-on-overflow.why_wrong: Mechanical substitution in the overflow branch. Tests that the suite distinguishes the sentinel 0 from no value at all, which the harness renders as an empty line.

t2-sign-comparison-inverted.why_wrong: Mechanical inversion of the sign ternary. Tests that the suite pins the sign on positive inputs as well as negative ones - a suite containing only negative examples would miss it.

t2-returns-the-reversed-string.why_wrong: Mechanical removal of the int() normalisation. The statement's third worked example exists precisely to pin trailing-zero handling, and this checks the suite actually enforces it rather than accepting a leading-zero rendering.
